title: Current, number density and drift speed

learning_outcomes.text: use, for a current-carrying conductor, the expression I = Anvq, where n is the number density of charge carriers

prior_knowledge_summary: Electric current is the rate of flow of charge.
Electrons are mobile charge carriers in metals.
Use Q = It and Q = Ne with e = 1.60 × 10^-19 C.
new_learning: Number density is the number of mobile carriers per unit volume.
Mean drift speed connects microscopic carrier motion to macroscopic current.

blocks.heading: How can slow electrons produce a current at once?
content: A lamp responds quickly when a switch closes, yet the mean drift speed of electrons in its wire can be much less than a millimetre per second. How can a small drift speed still produce a useful current?
The answer depends on how many carriers occupy each cubic metre and how much wire area they cross together.

figure.purpose: Create the need to connect slow microscopic motion with macroscopic current.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch. Show a long metal wire already filled with electron dots, a switch closing, and a magnified section with very short drift arrows. Avoid a circuit-analysis diagram.
figure.alt_text: A wire already full of electrons has tiny drift arrows after a switch closes.

blocks.heading: Count carriers in a moving slab
content: Take a wire of cross-sectional area A. In time t, carriers with mean drift speed v move an average distance vt. They sweep through a slab of volume Avt.
If n is the number of carriers per cubic metre, the slab contains nAvt carriers. Each carrier has charge magnitude q, so the transferred charge magnitude is Q = nAvtq.

figure.purpose: Derive the carrier count from conductor geometry.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch. Draw a cylindrical wire with area A and a shaded slab of length vt. Annotate volume Avt, number density n and carrier count nAvt.
figure.alt_text: A shaded cylindrical slab of length vt contains nAvt charge carriers.

blocks.heading: From charge flow to I = Anvq
content: From Lesson 2, I = Q/t. Substitute Q = nAvtq: I = nAvtq/t. The time cancels, giving I = Anvq.
Formula to remember: I = Anvq. I is current in A, A is cross-sectional area in m², n is number density in m^-3, v is mean drift speed in m s^-1, and q is carrier charge magnitude in C.

figure.purpose: Show the derivation and unit roles without skipping the Lesson 2 link.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch. Use a vertical equation chain Q = nAvtq, I = Q/t, I = Anvq. Place a small unit card beside every symbol.
figure.alt_text: An equation chain derives I = Anvq from charge in a moving slab and current as charge per time.

blocks.heading: Calculate a drift speed safely
content: A wire carries 1.2 A. Its area is 2.0 × 10^-6 m², n = 7.5 × 10^28 m^-3 and q = 1.60 × 10^-19 C. Rearrange before substituting: v = I/(Anq).
Check the order of magnitude: a huge number density makes a small drift speed plausible.

figure.purpose: Teach unit-safe substitution and powers-of-ten handling.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch. Show a worked fraction with coefficients and powers of ten grouped separately, followed by the result and an order-of-magnitude check.
figure.alt_text: A worked calculation rearranges I = Anvq and obtains a small drift speed.

blocks.heading: What changes the current?
content: The equation is a product. A larger area lets more carriers cross side by side. A larger number density supplies more carriers per cubic metre. A larger drift speed moves the carrier population through the section faster. A larger carrier charge transfers more charge per crossing particle.

For the same material, n and q are fixed. If current is also fixed, a narrower wire requires a larger drift speed. This inverse relationship is often quickest to solve as a ratio before inserting numbers.

figure.purpose: Make proportional and inverse relationships visible.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch. Use four small comparison panels for A, n, v and q. Add a separate thick-versus-thin wire panel showing equal current and faster drift in the thinner wire.
figure.alt_text: Comparison panels show how each factor changes current and how a thin wire needs faster drift for equal current.

blocks.heading: Drift speed is not the speed of the electrical response
content: It feels natural to imagine one electron racing from the cell to the lamp. The wire is already full of mobile electrons. When the electric conditions change, carriers throughout the wire begin a small net drift.

The small mean drift speed describes net carrier motion. It does not mean the lamp waits for one electron to travel around the whole path. Detailed circuit response belongs later; here the safe conclusion is only that many carriers make a useful current possible even when v is small.

figure.purpose: Separate mean drift speed from the rapid establishment of current without importing Topic 10 methods.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch. Show a line of beads already filling a tube; a small push at one end produces small simultaneous shifts along the line. Label analogy only and note beads are not electrons.
figure.alt_text: A filled bead tube analogy shows small shifts throughout without one bead crossing the whole tube first.

blocks.heading: A reliable I = Anvq routine
content: First convert area to m² and identify the carrier charge magnitude. Next choose the unknown and rearrange symbolically. Then substitute n carefully, keeping powers of ten visible.
Use a ratio when most factors cancel. Use Q = It and Q = Ne only when a question links a time interval or carrier count to the drift model.
Stop at the conductor model. Potential difference, resistance, power and resistor networks are not needed here.

figure.purpose: Summarise formula selection, unit checks and the topic boundary.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch. Draw a flow chart: identify A,n,v,q; convert units; rearrange; substitute; check magnitude. Add an optional branch to Q = It then Q = Ne for time-linked questions.
figure.alt_text: A flow chart summarises drift-current calculation and an optional charge-transfer branch.

evidence_basis.p1_status: deferred by canonical lesson specification; no lesson assignment invented
evidence_basis.evidence_scope_note: Only I = Anvq, number-density and drift-speed leaves are used; circuit-resistance and power context is excluded.

concepts_taught: number density as carriers per unit volume
misconceptions_addressed: A useful current requires individual electrons to move rapidly through the full wire.
Cross-sectional diameter can be substituted directly as area.
Carrier charge sign should make drift speed negative in a magnitude calculation.
next_lesson_can_assume: Calculate number density from carrier count and conductor volume.
Use ratio cancellation for equal-current conductors.
Connect Q = It and Q = Ne to the drift model when time is supplied.
next_lesson_must_not_assume: Potential difference or energy per unit charge.
Resistance, Ohm's law or circuit-network methods.
